title: Mastery Challenge: Architecture
objective: After this level you can demonstrate command of Architecture Levels 1–99 across the whole tree.
summary: Questions from how buildings stand to how we build next: beams, arches, domes and chains, then green, timber, printed, floating, lunar and saved buildings. Every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: The Architecture Mastery Challenge.
cards.body: Ten questions, from how buildings stand to how we'll build next. Beams and arches, domes and hanging chains, timber towers, printed walls, floating houses and a base on the Moon. Take your time: every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: Architecture: mastered
learned: How new buildings keep heat in, let the sun help and grow plants on their roofs and walls.
Why thick timber can survive a fire, and why printed concrete walls still struggle with stretching.
Why old buildings get restored, protected or given new jobs, and why designing for all helps everyone.
How to read any building: what it's for, how it stands and how it has changed.

questions.prompt: In Vitruvius's three conditions, which word means a building is useful to the people in it?

options.label: Firmness
options.rationale: Firmness means strength.

options.label: Delight
options.rationale: Delight means beauty.

options.label: Commodity
Venustas
options.rationale: Venustas is the Latin for delight.

questions.explanation: Firmness is strength, commodity is usefulness to the people who use it, and delight is beauty.

questions.prompt: A long stone lintel over a wide gap cracks along its underside. Why there?

options.label: The underside is stretched, and stone is weak in tension
The underside is squeezed hardest of all
options.rationale: The top is squeezed; the underside is stretched.

options.label: Rainwater collects under the lintel
options.rationale: It's the bending, not the weather.

options.label: The posts pull the lintel apart sideways
options.rationale: The load bends it; the posts hold it up.

questions.explanation: A loaded beam is squeezed on top and stretched underneath, and brittle stone is weak in tension.

questions.prompt: A new stone arch's feet slide apart once its wooden frame is removed. Which push did its supports fail to resist?

options.label: Tension in the keystone
options.rationale: The keystone is squeezed, not stretched.

options.label: Thrust, the arch's outward push
Wind pressing on its side
options.rationale: The push came from the arch's own load.

options.label: Hoop forces in a dome's rings
options.rationale: Hoop forces belong to domes, Level 5.

questions.explanation: An arch pushes outward at its feet (thrust); supports must be massive enough to resist it.

questions.prompt: Why did Brunelleschi bind Florence's dome with tie rings?

options.label: To hang lamps inside the dome
options.rationale: The rings are structural.

options.label: To stop the top from being squeezed
options.rationale: Squeezing near the top is what holds each ring in place.

options.label: To hold in the lower part, where hoops stretch
So that the dome needed no bricks
options.rationale: The dome is masonry; the rings bind it.

questions.explanation: Lower down, a dome's hoop forces stretch; tie rings act like barrel hoops holding in the part that wants to spread.

questions.prompt: ESA's 2013 Moon base study used a catenary dome. In Hooke's terms from Level 10, what is a catenary arch?

options.label: A beam laid across two posts
options.rationale: That's post and lintel, Level 3.

options.label: A ring of stone held by metal cramps
options.rationale: That's a tie ring, Level 5.

options.label: A skeleton of columns and beams
options.rationale: That's a frame, Level 8.

options.label: A hanging chain's curve, turned upside down

questions.explanation: "As hangs the flexible line, so but inverted will stand the rigid arch." A catenary is that hanging curve.

questions.prompt: In winter, what does a heat recovery ventilator do with the warm, stale air leaving a house?

options.label: Uses its heat to warm the fresh air coming in
Keeps it inside, so no fresh air is needed
options.rationale: Fresh air still comes in; only the heat is kept.

options.label: Sends it straight out through an open window
options.rationale: That throws the heat away.

options.label: Stores it inside the thick walls
options.rationale: Walls store heat, not stale air.

questions.explanation: In a heat exchanger, heat moves from the warm outgoing air to the cold incoming air.

questions.prompt: Besides its mass timber, what is Milwaukee's Ascent tower built on?

options.label: A steel skeleton with walls of fired brick
options.rationale: Its timber sits on concrete.

options.label: A concrete base and concrete elevator and stair shafts
A hollow concrete barge
options.rationale: That's a floating home, Level 95.

options.label: A shell of 3D-printed concrete
options.rationale: Its concrete was not printed.

questions.explanation: Ascent is a hybrid: concrete base and shafts, with 19 of its 25 stories in mass timber.

questions.prompt: A concrete printer needs no formwork. Which temporary support from Level 4 plays a similar role for an arch?

options.label: The keystone
options.rationale: The keystone stays; it's the last stone set.

options.label: The massive supports at its feet
options.rationale: Those stay to resist the thrust.

options.label: Centering, the wooden frame under the arch
Tie rings of stone and oak
options.rationale: Those bind Florence's dome for good.

questions.explanation: Formwork holds wet concrete until it hardens; centering holds an arch up until its keystone is set.

questions.prompt: At Maasbommel, how does an amphibious house differ from a floating one?

options.label: It has no mooring posts at all
options.rationale: Both slide on mooring posts.

options.label: It is built entirely of steel
options.rationale: It stands on a hollow concrete base.

options.label: It never floats, even in a flood
options.rationale: It floats when the river rises.

options.label: It rests on a foundation until the river rises

questions.explanation: Amphibious homes rest on concrete foundations and float when the river rises; floating homes are concrete barges.

questions.prompt: The SPAB's 1877 manifesto asked people to put what in the place of Restoration?

options.label: Protection
Reconstruction
options.rationale: Rebuilding was the opposite of what Morris wanted.

options.label: Demolition
options.rationale: The society existed to save old buildings.

options.label: Modernization
options.rationale: The manifesto asked for daily care, not updating.

questions.explanation: "Put Protection in the place of Restoration, to stave off decay by daily care."
